articles.title: Who decides how tax money reaches the states?
articles.subject: Polity & Economy
articles.excerpt: A state runs schools and hospitals, but not every tax goes into its own account. This is where the Finance Commission comes in.

sections.heading: Start with a school
paragraphs: A government school needs teachers, classrooms and money every year. The state pays for much of this work. Yet some major taxes are collected by the Union. How does part of that money reach the states?

Article 280 of the Constitution provides for a Finance Commission. The President constitutes it every five years, or earlier if necessary. Its job includes recommending how certain Union tax proceeds should be shared.

sections.heading: Two decisions, not one
paragraphs: First comes the division between the Union and the states. This is called vertical devolution. Next comes the division of the states’ share among individual states. That is horizontal devolution.

These are different questions. The first asks how large the states’ collective share should be. The second asks how to divide that share when states have different populations, incomes and spending needs. Do not confuse either with a grant for a particular programme.

sections.heading: What to watch in a news report
paragraphs: Check whether the report discusses the overall share, the formula between states, or grants. A change in one does not automatically mean a change in the others.

Also check the period covered. A percentage from one commission’s award should not be treated as a permanent constitutional rule. The Constitution creates the institution; its recommendations deal with a particular period. For an answer on federalism, explain the mismatch between who collects revenue and who delivers services before quoting a number.

articles.takeaway: Vertical devolution divides taxes between the Union and states. Horizontal devolution divides the states’ share among states.
articles.question: Why might equal shares for every state produce unequal public services?

sources.label: Constitution of India · Articles 270 and 280
sources.note: Start with Article 280(3)(a), which distinguishes distribution between the Union and states from allocation between states. Article 270 concerns the divisible pool.

sources.label: Finance Commission · reports and recommendations
sources.note: Open the report for the award period being discussed. Read the tax-devolution formula and grants separately; a homepage alone does not establish a current percentage.

example.heading: Follow ₹100 through two decisions
example.text: Imagine a divisible pool of ₹100. Suppose ₹40 is assigned to the states collectively. Choosing ₹40 is the vertical decision. If State A then receives ₹6 of that ₹40, that is part of the horizontal allocation. These numbers are invented to explain the mechanism; they are not a commission’s recommendation. A grant is a separate transfer and should not be added to either percentage without checking what the table measures.

comparison.heading: Share, allocation and grant
rows: Vertical devolution
How much of the divisible pool goes to the states together?
Horizontal devolution
How is that states’ share divided between individual states?
Grant
What additional assistance is recommended, and for what purpose?

articles.recallAnswer: States have different populations, revenue capacity and service costs. Giving each the same amount does not give each resident the same support. Explain the formula’s purpose before judging the result.

articles.title: The repo rate changed. Why hasn’t your loan?
articles.subject: Economy
articles.excerpt: A policy-rate decision is the start of a chain. Bank funding, loan terms and timing decide how far it travels.

sections.heading: The first link in the chain
paragraphs: You read that the Reserve Bank has cut the repo rate. A month later, your loan payment looks the same. That does not, by itself, mean the decision failed.

The policy repo rate is the rate at which the RBI provides overnight liquidity to banks against eligible collateral under its liquidity adjustment facility. It influences the cost of short-term money. It is not the interest rate printed on every borrower’s loan agreement.

sections.heading: The route to a household
paragraphs: Banks fund themselves through deposits and other borrowing, as well as central-bank facilities. Their lending decisions also reflect credit risk, operating costs and competition. A policy change works through these conditions rather than replacing them.

The loan contract matters too. A floating-rate loan may be linked to an external benchmark or a bank’s internal benchmark. Its reset schedule affects when the rate changes. A fixed-rate loan does not ordinarily move just because the policy rate does. Read the benchmark and reset clauses before expecting a lower payment.

sections.heading: The exam idea is transmission
paragraphs: Monetary transmission describes how a central-bank decision affects market rates, credit, spending and prices. It takes time, and the effect can differ across borrowers and sectors.

For a Mains answer, trace that chain and identify where it can slow down. For Prelims, keep the policy rate separate from a bank’s lending rate. Avoid turning a rate cut into a promise that every loan will become cheaper immediately.

articles.takeaway: A policy-rate change influences borrowing costs; the benchmark and reset terms determine when a particular loan responds.
articles.question: Which part of the transmission chain would you check before judging whether a rate cut worked?

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India · monetary policy
sources.note: Read the policy statement for the decision date. A policy-rate change is evidence about the first link, not every borrower’s interest rate.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India · frequently asked questions
sources.note: Use the relevant explanation of lending benchmarks and floating rates, then compare it with the actual loan agreement. A general FAQ index is a starting point.

example.heading: The next reset date matters
example.text: Suppose a floating-rate loan has a benchmark of 6% and a spread of 2%, giving a rate of 8%. If the benchmark falls to 5.75% and the spread stays the same, the rate becomes 7.75% when the contract resets. The figures are illustrative. Even then, the lender may change the tenure rather than the instalment, depending on the agreement. The useful documents are the loan’s benchmark, spread and reset clauses.

comparison.heading: Read the right rate
rows: Policy repo rate
The RBI’s policy decision and effective date.
Loan benchmark
The benchmark named in this particular contract.
Borrower’s rate
Benchmark plus spread, subject to the contract and reset schedule.

articles.recallAnswer: Check the loan’s benchmark and next reset date first. Then look at the spread and whether the lender adjusts the instalment or tenure. An unchanged instalment alone cannot measure transmission.

articles.title: A wetland is more than a place on a list
articles.subject: Environment
articles.excerpt: When a wetland enters the news, look beyond its designation. The useful question is what the water, land and people do together.

sections.heading: Think of the water first
paragraphs: Picture a low-lying area that holds water after rain. Depending on its ecology, it can slow runoff, support plants and animals, and sustain local livelihoods. Filling it may change where water goes during the next heavy shower.

Wetlands are varied. They include marshes, lakes and other ecosystems covered by the broad definition used in the Convention on Wetlands. They are not all freshwater, and they are not all untouched by people.

sections.heading: What a Ramsar designation tells you
paragraphs: A Ramsar site is a wetland designated as internationally important under the Convention. Its inclusion is useful information, but a label alone cannot tell you whether the site is healthy today.

The Convention’s idea of wise use concerns maintaining ecological character through ecosystem approaches within sustainable development. That calls for attention to water flows, pollution, habitat and how the surrounding landscape is used. It is not simply a ban on every human activity.

sections.heading: Make your notes explain something
paragraphs: Instead of copying a long list of sites, make a small note about one: its location, wetland type, ecological role and a documented pressure. Use a current site record for species and status, rather than assuming an old fact still applies.

For Mains, connect conservation to the people and institutions managing the catchment. A wetland can be protected on paper while upstream development changes its water supply. That relationship is more useful to understand than the designation alone.

articles.takeaway: Know the designation, then explain the ecosystem: water flows, ecological character, livelihoods and pressures.
articles.question: How could a land-use change outside a wetland affect the wetland itself?

sources.label: Convention on Wetlands · convention and wise use
sources.note: Find the Convention text: Article 1.1 defines wetlands, while Article 3.1 addresses conservation and wise use. Read wise-use guidance before equating it with a ban on use.

sources.label: Ramsar Sites Information Service · individual site records
sources.note: Search an individual site and read its Ramsar Information Sheet, including hydrology, ecological features and reported pressures. Check when the record was updated.

example.heading: A road can change a wetland without filling it
example.text: Imagine a wetland fed by seasonal runoff. A raised road across its catchment could interrupt a channel even if the wetland boundary is untouched. The investigation would follow water inflows and outflows, seasonal timing and the effect on habitat and livelihoods. This is a hypothetical situation, not a claim about a particular Ramsar site. It shows why protecting a boundary and maintaining ecological character are different tasks.

comparison.heading: Designation and condition
rows: Is it internationally designated?
The Ramsar designation and site record.
What kind of wetland is it?
Its habitat, hydrology and ecological description.
Is it healthy now?
Dated monitoring evidence, pressures and changes in ecological character.

articles.recallAnswer: A change in the catchment can alter inflow, sediment or pollution reaching the wetland. Follow the water across the boundary: a road that interrupts a channel may affect habitat even without filling the wetland itself.

articles.title: A Bill passed. Is the new rule in force?
articles.subject: Polity
articles.excerpt: Introduction, passage, assent and commencement describe different steps. A headline often tells you about only one of them.

sections.heading: Follow the stage, not just the headline
paragraphs: A news report says that Parliament has passed a Bill. It is tempting to write that the new rule now applies everywhere. Before doing that, check the legal stage.

A Bill is a proposal for legislation. For an ordinary Union Bill, agreement by both Houses is generally required, subject to the constitutional process for resolving a deadlock. Presidential assent is another step. Money Bills and constitutional amendments follow distinct procedures, so do not use one simple sequence for every case.

sections.heading: An Act can start later
paragraphs: Even after assent, you still need to check commencement. An Act may state that it begins immediately, specify a date, or allow the government to appoint a date by notification. Different provisions may begin on different dates if the law provides for that.

There may also be rules made under the Act. These provide details within the authority delegated by the legislation. The Act, its commencement notification and its rules answer different questions. Read the relevant documents together.

sections.heading: A small habit that prevents a big error
paragraphs: Write the stage beside the name in your notes: introduced, passed, assented to, or brought into force. If you cannot establish the last step, leave it open rather than guessing.

For Prelims, this helps you avoid treating a proposal as an existing legal duty. For Mains, it helps separate a policy announcement from implementation. The practical question is not only what the law says, but which provisions apply and what institutions must do to carry them out.

articles.takeaway: Passage, assent and commencement are separate checks. Read the commencement provision before saying a rule is in force.
articles.question: Which document would you look for if an Act lets the government choose its start date?

sources.label: Constitution of India · Articles 107–111
sources.note: Articles 107–111 set out parts of the Union legislative process. Money Bills have a distinct procedure; avoid applying one ordinary-Bill shorthand to every Bill.

sources.label: India Code · Acts and subordinate legislation
sources.note: Open the particular Act. Read its commencement section, then any commencement notifications and relevant rules. An Act’s presence in the database alone does not prove that every provision is in force.

example.heading: One Act, different start dates
example.text: Imagine an Act whose commencement clause allows the government to appoint dates by notification. A notification brings sections 1 to 5 into force, while the remaining sections wait. The Act has received assent, but a rule in section 8 has not started merely because the Act was published. This is an illustration. For a real law, read the exact commencement clause and the notifications naming the relevant section.

comparison.heading: Three documents, three checks
rows: Passage
The legislative record showing approval through the applicable procedure.
Assent
The enacted law and assent/publication record.
Commencement
The Act’s start-date clause and any notification it requires.

articles.recallAnswer: Look for the commencement notification issued under the Act’s start-date provision. Check its date and the sections it covers; one notification may not commence the whole Act.

articles.title: When GDP grows, how much is just higher prices?
articles.subject: Economy
articles.excerpt: A bigger rupee total can reflect more production, higher prices, or both. Real and nominal GDP help separate those stories.

sections.heading: Try a very small economy
paragraphs: Imagine an economy that produces only ten loaves of bread. Last year each loaf cost ₹20. This year it produces the same ten loaves, but each costs ₹25. The value rises from ₹200 to ₹250. Production has not increased.

This simplified example shows why a higher money total is not enough to establish growth in output. In an actual economy, statisticians must account for many goods and services, rather than one product.

sections.heading: Read the price basis
paragraphs: GDP at current prices is commonly called nominal GDP. It values production using the prices of the period being measured. GDP at constant prices is used to assess real growth by accounting for price changes relative to a base period.

So when a report quotes a growth rate, ask which measure it uses. Also check whether it compares a quarter with the same quarter a year earlier, or a full year with the previous year. A weak comparison period can make a later growth rate look especially large. This is the base effect.

sections.heading: What GDP cannot tell you on its own
paragraphs: GDP measures production within an economy. It does not, on its own, show how income is distributed or whether every household is better off. A national total and a household experience can move differently.

For a good answer, use the number for the question it can answer. Real growth helps discuss output. Per-capita figures add population context. Distribution, employment and other indicators are needed for broader claims about living standards. Always keep the reporting period and price basis beside the statistic.

articles.takeaway: Nominal growth includes price changes. Real growth helps isolate changes in output; neither alone describes everyone’s living standard.
articles.question: In the bread example, what happens to nominal output and to the quantity produced?

sources.label: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation · national accounts
sources.note: Go to National Accounts and open the dated estimate release being quoted. Check current versus constant prices, the base year, the comparison period and whether the estimate was revised.

example.heading: When both prices and quantity rise
example.text: Imagine 100 identical items at ₹10 each: output is worth ₹1,000. Next year, 110 items sell for ₹11 each, giving ₹1,210. Money value has risen by 21%, while quantity has risen by 10%. Measuring the second year’s 110 items at the starting price gives ₹1,100, which isolates the quantity change in this one-product illustration. Real national accounts cover many goods and services; these figures are invented to explain the distinction, not describe India’s growth.

comparison.heading: Do not swap these measures
rows: GDP at current prices
Changes in money value, including price changes.
GDP at constant prices
Output changes measured using a common price basis.
GDP per person
Aggregate output relative to population, without describing its distribution.

articles.recallAnswer: Nominal output rises because the bread costs more, while the quantity produced stays the same. Higher money value alone does not establish an increase in the amount of output.
